**Verdict:** Yes. Admit the real flaws your prospects already think about, and do it in the ad itself. Hormozi says "nothing more powerful than damaging admissions," and "trust trumps promise," so you give up some promise to gain trust.

**Based on:** said it (confidence: high). He addresses this directly and has a named tactic for it.

**Why he'd say it**
- Admitting bias makes people believe you more. He cites unnamed research for this, and his Eminem rap-battle story is an illustration, not data of his own. "you want to always own your flaws of course you have them of course your product isn't perfect say so" ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=750s), 12:30)
- Prospects are already thinking the flaw. If you claim it first, you get the trust and they stop holding it against you. "write down all of the flaws all the things that people complain about the things that you know you could do better and claim them" ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=903s), 15:03)
- Referrals work the same way. You don't need much promise when someone trusts you, so you give up promise in exchange for trust. ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=789s), 13:09)

**How to word it**

The structure is *true damaging thing, but the claim you want believed.* He's explicit that the words after "but" are what the reader takes away: "the statement that comes after the word but is the part that is the thing you want them to believe" (13:44).

His own examples, from the same talk:
- "our websites are ugly as hell but they convert"
- "our gym honestly has pretty terrible parking… but our sessions are more fun than everyone else's"

Rules he gives:
- Keep the admission true and specific. Vague or fake flaws don't work, since "anyone can say that" and the prospect doesn't believe it (16:15).
- Pick flaws the buyer already complains about, not ones they've never noticed.
- Make the "but" the benefit that matters, and keep it concrete.
- Use humor if you can. He calls it "bonus points" (15:39).
- Keep the promise you actually make. He doesn't say to drop it, only to lead with the admission.

For your product, the pattern is: "[the flaw buyers already mention], but [the outcome you want them to remember]." I don't know your product, so I can't draft the real lines. If you tell me the flaws customers complain about, I'll draft a few in this form. Those drafts would be my adaptation, not his words.

**What would change their answer**
- On sales calls, he goes further: he front-loads the downsides, then the benefits, so the prospect can self-qualify. "Listen, before I tell you about the good, let me tell you about the bad." ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH-IMJxbUY4&t=1182s), 19:42). If the flaw is a dealbreaker for the buyer you want, he'd still disclose it, since that's how the wrong buyer leaves.
- He treats this as a copy tactic for prospects who already know the flaw. It doesn't cover hiding a flaw that matters more than the one you're admitting.
- Discount this a little for self-interest: he sells the books and courses where this tactic is taught, and his evidence for the persuasion effect is anecdote plus an unnamed study.

**Verdict:** Hormozi's benchmark is 80% monthly retention (20% churn), with under 10% churn as best. Worry when fewer than 7 in 10 members stay each month, and read churn by tenure cohort, not as one blended average.

**Based on:** said it. He addressed this exact question in one 2026 video, which uses Skool platform data. The thresholds below come from that video, not from a set of talks.

**What he'd check, in order**

1. **Joins vs. cancels every month.** "track those two numbers on a monthly basis, joins versus cancels, and then force yourself to label the businesses growing, flat, or declining based on that" ([source](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=33s) @ 0:33). If cancels exceed joins, recurring revenue is shrinking.
2. **Benchmarks.** "the platform average across School is 80% monthly retention. So said differently, it's 20% churn." "The best groups have less than 10% churn." "The not good groups have less than 70% retention, aka 30% or higher" ([source](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=99s) @ 1:39).
3. **Tenure.** "month one to three are the highest churn. So, they're 20% plus during these months. Now, if you keep someone 90 days… it drops to around 10% or less." By month six, "it goes from like 10% to 2%" ([source](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=233s) @ 3:53).

**When to worry**

- **Below 70% retention (over 30% churn) a month:** this is the main alarm. "if less than seven out of 10 people want to stay on a monthly basis, you probably need to work on your retention more than anything else. It'll be the highest ROI lever" ([source](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=99s) @ 1:39).
- **Month-one churn of 20%+ is normal:** "don't overhaul your entire business because your month one churn sucks," unless "basically everyone's leaving" ([source](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=264s) @ 4:24).
- **Young communities look worse than they are:** "if your community or recurring revenue thing is less than 90 days old, then your churn is always going to be inflated" ([source](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=264s) @ 4:24).
- **Churn that stays near 20% after day 90 is my inference, not his words:** he says churn should drop to around 10% by then, so a cohort still at 20% past day 90 is behind his benchmark and is where I'd look first.

**What he'd do about it**

- Get people past day 90 and month six, rather than chasing the blended average: "How do I get someone to stay past day 90? How do I get these people to stay past month six?" (same source, @ 4:24).
- Day 90 needs a result: "Day 90 is probably going to have to deliver some sort of outcome, some sort of change in behavior for them. Month six, it's usually them connecting with other people within that community" ([source](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=331s) @ 5:31).
- Message cancellers and tag their reasons. Overwhelm is "the number one reason people churn, outside of price" (@ 9:18).

**What would change his answer**

- The benchmarks are Skool platform averages, which he got from Skool's founder. He says they fit online and consumer services, not "an insurance premium or an alarm system." A high-ticket B2B community or one on annual contracts may not match these numbers.
- He has a stake in Skool, the platform the data comes from ([[profile]]). Treat the figures as a useful frame, not as independent evidence.
- The vault has no other source on community churn, so this rests on one video.

If you share your monthly joins, cancels and the age of the community, I can run the numbers against these thresholds.

**Verdict:** Pay the $60k off on a fixed schedule, and fix the cheap growth levers first. Hormozi would not spend growth cash to clear the debt early, but he also wouldn't let idle cash sit while a proven channel is available.

He'd say the debt is a risk that doesn't go away. Businesses have seasons and volatility, and "risk when multiplied over a long time horizon tends to come due." Paying it down also brings relief he calls "more of an emotional thing."

**Based on:** said it (for the $60k case) | follows from what they said for the cash-for-growth side (confidence: medium)

**How we get there**
1. The nearest case is almost your exact situation. A profitable HVAC service business with $60,000 of debt asked the same question. Hormozi said, "I tend to skew like very close to the Ramsey side," and endorsed paying it off in four to five months ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 8:37; https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=517s).
2. The rule behind that is that debt is risk, and risk comes due. He added, "why did I take the debt out to begin with? A lot of times it's cuz I wanted to grow faster" ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 9:10; https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=550s). ([[thinking/hormozi]])
3. The growth side is also his rule. He spends on ads only while returns hold: "we just want to continue to spend month over month provided our ROAS and our CAC stay more or less the same" ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 10:48; https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=648s). So growth cash goes to a channel with measured returns, not to a hope. In the consult, the ranked plan was a price raise first, then "continue to pay off the debt," then the funnel ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 30:45; https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=1845s). Growth moves that cost nothing come first.

**Why they'd say it**
- "Risk when multiplied over a long time horizon tends to come due." ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 9:10)
- "I'd say this is more of an emotional thing, but it's just this back of mind thing." ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 8:37)
- "You cannot take any risk on if you have no time and no money." ([[yt-jfW6gL6hKhk]] @ 13:04; https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk&t=784s). Cash is your capacity to take risk, so don't spend all of it on debt or on growth.

**What would change their answer:** He'd switch to keeping the cash if you had a channel with proven returns that you were already scaling, and paying the debt would starve it. He'd keep a buffer rather than go to zero. The vault doesn't say how big that buffer should be or how interest rates change the math. Hormozi's argument is about risk, not rate. If your debt is cheap and a proven channel returns more than the rate, the arithmetic favors keeping the cash. That's my read, not his, and the vault doesn't settle it.

**Caveats:** His debt view is a stated lean ("emotional," "skew close to Ramsey"), not a worked finance argument. He's pro-risk everywhere else, and the vault notes he doesn't reconcile the two ([[tensions]]). His consult business was about $1.2M a year in revenue, so check whether the scale fits yours.

**Verdict:** No. Raise prices about 10%. At an 82% close rate, Hormozi reads the price as too low, and his rule is that you come out ahead as long as the close rate stays above about 65%.

**Based on:** said it (confidence: high). He addressed a near-identical case: an HVAC duct-cleaning business at about $1.25M a year, a 38% net margin, and an 82% close rate ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4).

**Why they'd say it**
- Fear of the price is the mistake: "they're so afraid of charging money that they actually sell themselves out of a sale" ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 7:33, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=453s).
- A higher price raises trust in delivery. "if you raise your prices, what sometimes happens is that the conviction of the customer that you can actually deliver on the promise you're making goes up" ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 7:00, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=420s). He says this applies to a normal service, not a luxury good.
- The threshold: "whenever I hear 80% or over 80% close rates, I usually know that there's room in sale" and "As long as we close more than 65%, we make more money" ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 8:06, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=486s).
- The payoff: "10% price raise for you equals roughly a 25% increase in net profit" (same timestamp).

**What they've done:** In the same consult, the owner raised prices 23% after an earlier workshop recommendation, and Hormozi says that "resulted in a higher close rate and more money" ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 6:26, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=386s). He then made a 10% raise the first item on the priority list ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 30:45). The one-year follow-up reports revenue of about $2.3–2.5M and credits lead volume and marketing. It doesn't report the close rate or isolate the effect of price, so the pricing evidence is his claim plus one owner's anecdote.

**Checking the math on your numbers**
- Profit today is about $456K (38% of $1.2M). A 10% raise at the same volume with the same costs adds about $120K, to about $576K, or +26%. That matches his ~25%.
- His 65% comes from assuming every cost moves with each closed job. Under that assumption, break-even close rate = 82% × 0.38 / 0.48 ≈ 65%.
- If a large share of your 62% cost base is fixed (trucks, office, salaried staff), break-even rises. If everything were fixed, it would be about 74–75%. Work out how much of your costs really scale per job before you rely on 65%.
- Example, all costs per job: at a 75% close rate after a 10% raise, profit is about $526K, still above $456K.

**What would change their answer:** A close rate that falls below your real break-even after the raise. The vault also has a relevant rule: when ideal customers cite price, he adds a lower tier, but he ignores price complaints from people outside the target customer ([[tensions]], "Taking price complaints seriously").

**Where I'd push back:** His 65% is a rounded rule of thumb for one business, not a general law. The raise rests on one anecdote and his reasoning about trust. Before you roll it out everywhere, I'd test it for 4–6 weeks on a slice of new leads and track close rate against your break-even. Also keep in mind that these videos promote his roadmap and consulting, so discount them accordingly.

**Verdict:** Hormozi tells this as a story about skill stacking and where a skill is scarce. Bankers on an IPO roadshow told him his company would be worth four times more on the NASDAQ than on the European exchange it had just listed on. That led him to look for where his marketing and storytelling skills were scarce and paid best: companies heading into an IPO. He then took an equity deal for roughly nine to twelve months of work, which he says was worth about $7–8M on IPO day. That deal led to the company he now runs, Flight Story.

**Based on:** said it. This is from his 2023 appearance on *The Diary of a CEO* (raw source `yt-x3e73Qn6NOo`, [youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo)). The wiki doesn't cover it yet. Searches for NASDAQ, IPO, equity and valuation only hit the raw text.

**What he says happened**
1. **The bank pitch.** After a roadshow with about 20 investment banks, "they told me that our business would be worth four times more if it was just on a different stock market" (the NASDAQ), so he learned that moving the same business "would be worth four times more" ([[yt-x3e73Qn6NOo]] @ 1:34:12, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5652s).
2. **The pivot.** A couple of years later he "looked for an industry where my skill set was in least Supply but highest demand." He concluded that was social media marketing and storytelling for companies about to IPO, because "if you have a good story it can swing your valuation by hundreds of millions" ([[yt-x3e73Qn6NOo]] @ 1:34:43, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5683s).
3. **The equity deal.** He compares a local gym paying about a thousand dollars with a pre-IPO company where he could "take 7 million yeah as part of an equity deal" ([[yt-x3e73Qn6NOo]] @ 1:35:17, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5717s). The company was one whose IPO "listed at 3 billion" (the transcript says "3 billion um billions"). He values his stake, for "the 9 to 12 months work," at "in the region of 7 to8 million" on IPO day ([[yt-x3e73Qn6NOo]] @ 1:35:51, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5751s).
4. **Flight Story.** "That's ultimately why we started our company which is now called flight story," which he says began about a year and a half before the interview, starting in the IPO market and later moving into biotech ([[yt-x3e73Qn6NOo]] @ 1:36:23, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5783s).
5. **The recap.** Later he links it to capital as a form of leverage. Public markets hold "significantly more capital," so the same work gets "more zeros" ([[yt-x3e73Qn6NOo]] @ 1:45:47, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=6347s).

**What the story doesn't establish**
- **The 4x is a banker's claim, and the listing never changed.** The auto-captions garble some words ("Forex" is almost certainly "four x"). He says they were "considering an IPO in another country," so the NASDAQ move was a hypothetical, not a result. Investment banks earn fees on listings, so their valuation pitch has a motive. That is my inference, not something he says.
- **The companies aren't clearly identified.** He says "my company went public" in Europe, then refers to "the first company I worked with" for the equity deal. The vault doesn't say whether these are the same company. The profile doesn't mention this IPO work at all.
- **The $7–8M is a recollection.** He says the share price fluctuated and calls the value "between depends." He gives both "9 to 12 months" and "nine months" for the work.

Do you want me to file this as a `derived/` answer, or should we curate it into the wiki first? Wiki pages are curated with you, so I'd wait for your go-ahead before writing there.

**Verdict:** He didn't. In the roofing video, Hormozi told the owner to go all in on door-to-door as the primary growth engine, and to build a team of door-knocking reps. The Google Ads advice in the vault comes from a different business, an HVAC cleaning client.

**Based on:** said it (the roofing video, `yt-o64cI6tebnU`)

**Why he said it**
- The owner was two months old, at about $20K a month, and closed roughly one sale per 20 doors. Hormozi's reasoning was to put limited time and money behind the highest-return channel the owner was already good at: "I want to focus all efforts on the highest return stuff that you can do right now." ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU&t=196s))
- He treats the skill as rare: "knowing how to go get money is one of the ways to do that." ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU&t=229s))
- On scale: "Now I think that in terms of scale, you should go all in door to door." ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU&t=589s))
- Then: "It's what you're good at." and "I don't think we need to be cute about this." ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU&t=621s))
- The growth plan was a commission per door knocked, so income tracks effort. The illustration was $10 per door: 10% of a hoped-for $4K repair ticket, spread over an assumed 50 doors per sale for hired reps.

**What he did:** he kept door-knocking as the engine and told the owner to build a rep army. He also paired it with a VSL to handle objections, a maintenance membership, the menu upsell, and speed fees. In the 90-day follow-up, the guest reported revenue going from under $32K to about $247K. The unit isn't stated, and the figures are self-reported.

**Where Google Ads does come up:** in a different video (`yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4`) about an HVAC cleaning client. There he ranked fixes by cost and speed: price first, then the ad landing page, then ad spend, with outbound to HOAs last. That is an incremental-improvement sequence for a profitable business, not a switch away from door-knocking. Ad spend appears there at [4:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=259s) and in the ranked list at [30:45](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=1845s).

**What would change his answer:** the stated premise is wrong, so there is nothing to change. For this kind of owner, the condition that would move him off door-knocking is a channel that returns more per hour and that the owner already closes well. The vault doesn't say what he'd do once door-knocking stops scaling.

Two small notes: the wiki says "Caleb" and the video description says "Kaleb" for the owner's first name. The wiki's account of the roofing video is based on the captions, and the speaker attribution for one line is medium confidence.
